newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: Two days of Bangui clashes kill more than a dozen.
newsitem.headline: Two days of Bangui clashes kill more than a dozen.

text.p: Two days of clashes between African peacekeepers and disaffected soldiers killed more than a dozen people in the capital of the Central African Republic but died down after nightfall on Saturday, witnesses said.

They spoke of at least 10 killed on Saturday and four on Friday, including a Senegalese peacekeeper. Five of those wounded on Saturday were French nationals working at their embassy compound, which was hit by two stray mortar bombs.

France's ambassador to Bangui, Jean-Marc Simon, told a French television network that mortars had apparently been fired from a stronghold of the disaffected soldiers towards a camp of forces loyal to President Ange-Felix Patasse.
"One of the staff will have to be repatriated to France...because he has shrapnel in his lungs," he told the La Chaine Info television by telephone from Bangui.

The African peacekeeping force, deployed under a January 25 peace deal, has been touted as a model for a force to restore peace to Brazzaville, capital of the neighbouring Congo Republic where similar ethnic and political clashes broke out on June 5.
Brazzaville was relatively quiet on Saturday, the first day of an extended truce between supporters of President Pascal Lissouba and those of his predecessor Denis Sassou Nguesso.

Saturday's Bangui clashes focused on suburbs where the soldiers, principally from the southern Yakoma tribe of former military leader Andre Kolingba, enjoy popular support. The soldiers have yet to rejoin their units after three army mutinies in less than a year.
Friday's clashes were the first since a failed June 13 attempt to reintegrate mutineers from the paramilitary gendarmerie into their units under the January peace plan.
Mali's respected former military leader, Amadou Toumani Toure, who brokered the deal, was expected back in Bangui.

Mutinies in April and May 1996 began as protests over pay but became a movement to topple Patasse, a northern civilian elected in 1993. The third mutiny began in November and degenerated into ethnic bloodshed.

French troops, in the country under a defence pact, restored order after the latest mutiny and handed over to the peacekeepers. The African force includes soldiers from Burkina Faso, Chad, Gabon, Mali, Senegal and Togo.
